utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, Lisa Biersay, Case Manager Thomas Laugel and legal intern Marina Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with legal intern Sunna Aevarsdottir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, I remind you that you're still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a question -- we'll discuss a topic that was a subject of cross-examination, and it has to do with Osijek. Just for the record, it's the 22nd of July, page 10.113; 23rd of July, pages 10.200 and 10.221; the 24th of July, pages 10.240 up until 10.319. There has been a lot of talk about Osijek here, and you discussed it at length. What I wanted to ask you is this: Did the government of SBWS have the information and did it take part in any plans to take this town militarily?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the government was not informed about this, nor did anyone ever discuss that topic with the government or address the government in relation to it. None of the relevant factors, either military or civilian authorities. That was never a subject of discussion before the government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that is to say, 1992, 1993, at that time, to the best of your knowledge, the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or, rather, the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, did they have any plans to attack this town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can assert that with great certainty. And I can say with great certainty that while I was president of the RSK, to the best of my knowledge, and according to my information, not a single shell was fired at Osijek, at least not by the regular forces that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, during the cross-examination by the Prosecution, you gave quite a few answers, but I'd just like to ask you one more thing. Is there anything left that you wanted to say during the cross-examination that you did not get to say, either because you were interrupted by the Prosecutor or by me or due to some other reasons or circumstances?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps only two things. I forgot one the day before yesterday when I was answering your question and another thing I'd like to clarify is as follows: In response to the question put by the honourable Prosecutor concerning the visit of Madam Albright to Borovo Naselje. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but it seemed to me that he was imputing that I had invited Milan Ilic. Although that doesn't really matter. I think what matters that the truth should be known. The American embassy from Zagreb agreed on a visit to the local Serbs, and they agreed directly with Milan Ilic that he would be the host and I was subsequently invited by them and I took part in resolving that problem. So it is important for the Trial Chamber to know that if that is it relevant for any reason whatsoever. It is important that they know that this meeting had been agreed upon without any effort on my part. Also, in response to my -- to your question put two days ago, I didn't remember, I thought that you asked what was discussed at Mr. Simovic's on a particular day. I didn't remember. I said that Mr. Simovic had invited me but he was in this package of these contacts of ours when we had meetings with Mr. Wijnaendts and these preparations in Belgrade, preparing to go to The Hague and Paris twice. So it was at Simovic's office that we had these consultations rather than at the Serbian government building. And Jovic was there too and I think I was there with him once and another time Babic and Dzakula were there. And then he familiarized us with the problem of the Blue Helmets and Simovic in a way provided us with a service, some assistance and information before our trip to Paris and The Hague and that is why I went there. So as far as I can remember, that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hadzic. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution had intended to request just a few minutes, ten to 15 for, I think, just two matters now. One of them has actually been resolved by agreement with counsel on the admission of one of the items that were raised with the Chamber on Monday. So we would respectfully request leave to spend about ten to 15 minutes with Mr. Hadzic by way of re-cross on two topics. And then I would like to tender into evidence a few items that did not get tendered during the cross. This was raised on Monday, Your Honour, with Judge Hall, who suggested that we should consult with the Defence to see whether we could reach agreement on those and we have consulted and we have reached agreement as to all of them but one, and so my intention would just be simply to tender those, so I think just ten to 15 minutes should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I could correct Mr. Stringer: We reached agreement to all of them but two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll see about that. Yes, Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just a couple of items based on what was said yesterday, actually, during your redirect examination and one is just to clarify. You were asked again about an earlier stage of your examination when, actually, Judge Hall had asked you when did you become aware, when did you learn that Arkan was a criminal, that he was wanted by Interpol. And you spoke about that yesterday, and you again mention, as you had in the past, that you linked this to the time-frame in which Arkan became a media personality. What you told Judge Hall was that, you said and this is at 10157: "I can't remember exactly when that was but certainly it became known when Arkan became a media personality when foreign journalists came, the Australian consul came to visit him as well." And I now we have since corrected that reference to Australian Member of Parliament instead of Australian consul. Is that how it was, that was the time-frame in which you link your knowledge or your learning that Arkan had a criminal background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if just could be clarified this term "learned." And "knowledge" or "learned". I -- I think that this it is, in a way, compound. I think it's not the same, "knowledge" and "learn".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The question from His Honour Judge Hall was: "When did you learn that Arkan was a criminal, that he was wanted by Interpol?" So my question, Mr. Hadzic, is whether you link that learning to the time of the visit of the Australian prime minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never there, the Australian prime minister. That's the interpretation I received. I assume that's a slip of the tongue. There are two things that I have to clarify here. First of all, I understood His Honour Judge Hall properly, I think, because, first, the Prosecutor and I had this dispute about my interview with Mr. Dzuro in 2002 and Judge Hall intervened very cleverly and asked about the essence of the misunderstanding. When I said that whether I knew at the time in 2002 that Arkan was a criminal, and I said, yeah, and now the rest is all debatable what knowledge means, what learning means. To this day, I haven't received any official document from any institution stating that Arkan was a convicted criminal. Except when I came here to the Detention Unit then I got some of these judgements of his but when I'm speaking, I'm speaking about when I was free. I learned about him from the Croatian media and I didn't know any of that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Hall asked you, he said: "But, Mr. Hadzic, I do understand your testimony to be that back in 1991, you didn't know that Arkan was wanted by Interpol et cetera however at the time of the interview with Mr. Dzuro did you know?" And then he says: "My question is when did you learn that Arkan was a criminal that he was wanted by Interpol?" And, Mr. Hadzic, injure response to Judge Hall was: "You understood me very well. In 2002, I told Mr. Dzuro that I'd -- I knew that when I was talking to him -- I knew that when I was talking to him. As for the time when I learned that, I can't remember exactly when that was, but certainly it became known when Arkan became a media personality when foreign journalists came, the Australian consul came to visit him as well." So, Mr. Hadzic, you're linking this to the visit of the Australian gentleman, and my question is - and I'll finish my question, if I may - the question -- I just want to lock down the time-frame in which that occurred. My suggestion is that we're talking about January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to this question. First of all, this part of transcript was read to Mr. Hadzic twice today by Mr. Stringer, and I -- I think that he already asked -- already answered to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I respectively disagree, Mr. President. I don't think Mr. Hadzic answered at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to put it to you this way, Mr. Hadzic. In response to Judge Hall, you made a reference to media and the visit of the Australian gentleman. Can we agree that this occurred in January of 1992, the Australian gentleman's visit that we saw in the video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree. And I have to explain something here. I thought that my words were understood correctly but obviously they are not. I did not directly link that visit to knowing that Arkan was a criminal. I just said that the visit confused me additionally. When I saw that a high official of an UN member country was coming to see him and I had information from the Croatian media that he was a criminal so I thought that was not correct. I thought he was not a criminal because the Australian MP came to visit him because it seemed the other way around to me. If the Australian MP came to see him that meant that he was not a criminal. I never received any specific information from anyone about any kind of criminal activity of his and I didn't even know that he had served time in prison, if he was a criminal. He came with the police from Serbia as part of that system, and I thought that Serbia, as a member of the UN, was duty-bound to arrest criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Hadzic, that by January of 1992 Mr. Raznjatovic, Arkan, was, indeed, a well-known figure in the media?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he appeared in the media often. I didn't even have the possibility to follow all of that, there was no electricity, but he was relatively well-known towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last thing I want to ask you about, Mr. Hadzic, relates to your testimony about a video-clip that you were shown -- or, actually, you were asked to comment on, which is the video-clip that you commented on as P58, and it is the one in which you were asked at the end about whether Serbs and Croats can live together and it's the video in which your answer was -- you responded: "Not the brotherhood and unity type of co-existence introduced 50 years ago." That was the video you were asked about by my learned friend yesterday and that's the one I just want to follow up on now. Because in response to the question from your counsel, then, yesterday, what you said was that -- and this is at page 10830. Counsel asked: "In that interview and generally at the time was there any distinction between the Croats, judging by the place they were coming from and the like?" And you said: "No, that never existed." And you were then asked by Mr. Zivanovic: "I mean, it was a month or two after your interviews which I have shown you so it's war already, the war was raging one could say. Did you give such statements relating to Croats hailing from Herzegovina or some other area?" And your answer was: "Not at all. Nor did anyone try to establish this on the ground. My statements that were quite sharp in September, I didn't even have a telephone at the time. I said that because Stipe Mesic and that side were pointing their fingers at us." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I just wanted to follow up on it because it gave -- could give the impression that you were using sharp language, sort of at a time when -- when things were very heated, in terms of war or conflict with the Croat side, is that the message that you were trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I mentioned Stipe Mesic, I took him as an example but there were other politicians too who, at the time, gave statements against the Serbs so I was responding to them. At that time Mercep [phoen] said that only shovels were good enough for Serbs, that Serbs could no longer be managers in Croatia, that they could only be involved in public works and so on. Tudjman said then that he was glad that his wife was not a Serb or a Jew. In my view, such statements were pro-Fascist, so I said this in order to respond to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have P84.50, which is tab 701.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I want to take you to something that you said quite a bit later, in July of 1993. This is in an interview that you gave to the publication Borba. It's dated 24/25 July 1993, interview with Goran Hadzic, leader of the Krajina Serbs by Branislav Gulan in Erdut and Dalj. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I would object to the use of this document. It was not used in my re-direct or in the cross-examination. Mr. Hadzic saw it is completely new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the -- the part of Mr. Hadzic's testimony, Your Honour, that I just referred to indicated that he was using sharp language in September about the Herzegovina Croats. The point of this is to show that the sharp language isn't just linked to what was happening at the time, at the heat of the conflict in the fall of 1991. It continued for quite some time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution could prove it through his cross-examination and to use this document if he wanted to prove anything about action and conduct of the accused, so I object to the use of this document to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then, what's left is to tender a few documents into evidence, and the first of these is exhibit -- well, we are tendering 65 ter 1D03021.1 and that is simply a redacted version that we have made of what's already in evidence as D134. And counsel and I have conferred, and the Defence agrees that 3021.1 could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next one, Mr. President, and this came up yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, 1D03021.1 will be Exhibit D134.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, Your Honour, is from Mr. Hadzic's suspect interview, and this was used by both parties during the respective examinations. It is a seven-page excerpt of the suspect interview that relates to Mr. Hadzic's statements to Mr. Dzuro in relation to the people from Klisa who were -- who were brought to the training centre and the inquiries that were made after them. And we tendered this on Monday. This was another one Judge Hall suggested we confer and after conferring, the parties agree that we can tender into evidence 65 ter 4974.08J, which is the seven-page excerpt that capturing everything that Mr. Hadzic said on the Klisa issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 04974.08J will be Exhibit P3239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that one should be under seal, Mr. President, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next ones are documents 1D03606. It's agreed that that can be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D03606 will be Exhibit P3240, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 65 ter exhibit 6521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 6521 will be Exhibit P3241, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And 65 ter 6561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 6561 will be Exhibit P3242.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The last one, Mr. President, is one the parties disagree. But the Prosecution would tender two additional excerpts, both are very short, from the suspect interview that relates -- relate to the other incident. The Pap family. The Sinasi family incident in paragraph 27. This was shown to Mr. Hadzic -- it was used with Mr. Hadzic during the cross-examination, 4974.09B, and 4974.08F as in Fox, and so we tender these excerpts, again for impeachment purposes. That way, the Chamber will just have the entirety of it, as it relates to this one incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We object to these two -- two last exhibits. First of them, 4974.09B, we did not see any relevance for -- in this particular case to -- to tender this particular part of his interview. And as for 4974.08F, in -- as far as we could see this part was already in the exhibit 4974.08 -- 08J. And we see that it would be duplication of these parts of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit number you're mentioning, Mr. Zivanovic? 497 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a part of 4974.08J. In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- the Exhibit J has -- has the parts -- this part from Exhibit F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And that's an exhibit number. If is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is admitted as an exhibit; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not admitted. J is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel's correct. 08F, or at least part of it is in 08J, which was just admitted. This is just because there is overlap in the suspect interview. The way that Mr. Dzuro organised his questions for Mr. Hadzic, we felt like it's cleaner with 08J being sort of devoted to the Klisa incident, even though it does contain part of something that's relevant for the other case. And then we respectfully would, again, tender these two excerpts and have those be devoted toward the paragraph 27 incident. And I would, if I may, respond to counsel's first objection on relevance of .09 B, we strongly disagree; we think it's highly relevant. It's in this passage where Mr. Dzuro reads part of a statement to Mr. Hadzic that describes an incident of beating one of the annex victims and it continues on to talk about -- well, our submission is that the -- the entirety of the evidence that Mr. Dzuro put to Mr. Hadzic at the time was plenty of evidence to put him on notice and to focus him on the incident itself. And so we think for completeness everything that was said to Mr. Hadzic about the incident should be in the record, and that's what 4974.09B is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that everything contained in the Exhibit B was put to Mr. Hadzic during his cross-examination and it is in the transcript, and because of that, I think it is not -- it could not -- it is irrelevant for -- to tender this part of -- of evidence. As to Exhibit F, I would say that the only -- only difference between F and J is in that -- that in J, in Exhibit J, Mr. Hadzic hold Milosevic indictment in his hand when he responded to the question of the -- of Mr. Dzuro. And in F - and it was explored during the cross-examination - he didn't have this part of -- of video has no -- did not depict that Mr. Hadzic had the indictment from Milosevic in his hand when he answered to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Mr. President. On 09B we didn't read the entire thing to Mr. Hadzic; we read the parts that we thought -- we figured most prominently but as things developed we felt like, in the end, it's better for the Chamber to have everything that related to the incident that so that it can compare and conclude for itself the extent to which Mr. Hadzic would have been in a position to comment on this. As for 4974.08F it would be easier, just if we could quickly bring up page 13 of it on the screen than way the Chamber can see what counsel and I are probably both referring to here. Counsel has just made a reference to the Milosevic indictment. 4974.08F.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On page 13 of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, did I hear you well? I think I did, that you said in the beginning of this long discussion that those two documents are tendered for impeachment purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That's the basis they were tendered for on Monday. The point being that we feel the Chamber could be in a position best -- in a position to compare Mr. Hadzic's description of these incidents during his own testimony here with what he said back when Mr. Dzuro asked him about these and form the conclusions whether, in fact, Mr. Hadzic's recitation or his story is truthful today or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, a short and simple answer would be most helpful. It's for impeachment purposes; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The -- unless you want to add something, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, I would answer to this last exchange with Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please answer to the yes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't have comment about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I mean, the -- if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to -- to give the argument as to impeachment purpose from the point -- as to -- explained by Mr. Stringer as to Exhibit B. Because he said -- he actually said that some parts of this -- this document was not read to Mr. Hadzic, and if it is relevant for the impeachment, it had to be shown to the witness and it had to be addressed by Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, do you have a response to this last remark of Mr. Zivanovic? Has it been shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It was not -- all seven pages of it were not read into the record, Mr. President. That's true. We did present the parts that we thought that were the most significant. We didn't read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you want it to be read out to the witness now, while he is still on the stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the Prosecution had to do it during its cross-examination, and if they did not do it, just -- eventually just the read part of transcript -- or of this document could be tendered for the impeachment purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, please read to the witness the parts that have not been put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can remember exactly which parts I did put and which parts I didn't, as I stand here right now, Your Honour. I'll do my best. And I believe we need to go into private session for this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, I should have asked you before going into open session, but you'll tell me whether we -- we are good.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] can we do it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] okay. Further re-examination by Mr. Zivanovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, following up on the Prosecutor's questions about the Australian MP, or the ambassador as he was described here, or consul, I'm not going to read what you said and what the Prosecutor has already read out to you, but listen to your answer carefully, to the answer to my questions that I put to you yesterday. You will find that on page 10.780, starting on page -- on line 24. Please listen carefully because I will expect you to answer my questions later. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... let us clarify one thing. I think this -- your answer that is recorded in the transcript, you already said that, namely, that this is not a visit of the Australian consul, that this was actually a Member of Parliament, of the Australian parliament so when I put the question about the Australian consul, we don't have to correct that now. What I'm interested in is it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... context in which you mentioned. This visit of the Australian consul in view of the question that was put to, was this in the context of Arkan having become a media star or is the context your knowledge of him being a criminal? In other words, at that time of the visit of the Australian visitor, or the Australian consul or Member of Parliament had you heard by that that Arkan was a criminal or did you find out only later? "A. I cannot be very precise, but can I tell you what my understanding of it was? I said that there were a lot of controversies and I saw that he was being visited by a visitor from Australia, although it is not in the west. Australia for me is part of the west. Then I thought he was not a criminal. I mean I didn't have any document corroborating the stories that were being bandied about and there were journalists there, journalists of the world media, I mean, rich media if -- can I put that way. At world level. They talked to him and I thought if what people were saying were true, these journalists would not be talking to him. I didn't really deal with Arkan. I had problems of my own, but in 1991, I couldn't have known anything about him, whether he was a criminal, whether he was not a criminal or, rather, these activities of his and I did not know that he had been in prison in the west because of his crimes. I mean, if he serves his sentence then he becomes an innocent man and if he is a host of an Australian MP and if he acts host to the mayor of Belgrade, if one says that he is a colonel of the state security of the SFRY, I could not discern myself what was true and what was not true. "Q. All right. When you answered the question, when did you hear that Arkan was a criminal and that he was a wanted man by Interpol, what did you think this meant, "heard" when it says "heard"? "A. The media, whether I had read about that in Croatian newspapers, to be more specific, and they didn't have to be correct because the Croatian media were saying that everybody were criminals. Everybody on the other side, on our side, that is, so I could not be believe them. "Q. Does this mean that practically the source of your information about this, namely, that Arkan was a criminal is actually something that you first read about in the Croatian media and then you realised that he was a wanted man by Interpol? "A. Yes." I'll not read some exchange between the Prosecution and the Chamber and me, and I resume with page 10.783, line 23: "Q. Just like to go back to that question of mine that I put to you in the beginning. It was to do with your answer when you mentioned the visit of the Australian MP. Did you mention that in the context of Arkan becoming a media star, or did you mention it in the context that you knew at the time that he was a criminal or, rather, that he was a wanted man by Interpol? "A. No, no. I did not know then that he was wanted by Interpol because of that visit. This ambassador, or, rather, this Member of Parliament came to see him as if he were a media star, and I was confused by that. When I heard that he was a criminal, I started wondering how could the representative of a serious country come and visit a criminal? I said that in that context. "Q. Perhaps my question was unclear. Perhaps you misunderstood or perhaps it was misinterpreted" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise, Mr. President, especially since the Chamber's given the Prosecution so much of the floor this morning. We don't see the point of re-reading Mr. Hadzic's testimony into the record from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to -- to -- to recall Mr. Hadzic about his testimony and to put him -- the question related to the question of the Prosecution on today's questions related to the -- to his knowledge about Arkan was a criminal and wanted by the Interpol. I'd just like to remind him what was said exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think, actually, Mr. Zivanovic, that Mr. Hadzic has a perfect memory and knows what he said yesterday. How much do you want to read more to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just have to -- to finish that page, and two -- two -- two lines of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Reluctantly, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, by all means --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: By all means, I'm looking at the clock, we're not going into the next hearing with this, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. "Q. Perhaps my question was unclear. Perhaps you misunderstood or perhaps it was misinterpreted you said I'm reading line 21 in English know then that he was wanted by Interpol because that visit [Interpretation] I did not ask you whether he was a wanted man by Interpol because of the visit but at the time of the visit, did you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I gave a proper answer than it was misinterpreted. I said at the time of the visit I did not -- that he was a wanted man by Interpol and I was particularly confused when I heard about this and I thought these were rumours. A man, a serious man from the European Union would not come and visit him then. I think that Serbia or Yugoslavia as a member of Interpol should arrest anyone who was wanted by Interpol. "Q. So when did you hear that? Can you assess that? Can you assess that when it was that you, taking into account that visit by the Croatian ambassador or I'm sorry, the Australian ambassador? "A. Not ambassador, Member of Parliament. "Q. Member of Parliament. "A. I do not know. During 1992, I cannot be very specific. "Q. Thank you." That's it. [Interpretation] To follow up on a question put to you earlier today by the Prosecutor, tell us again, during the visit of the Australian MP, did you know that Arkan was a criminal wanted by Interpol, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I did not know that he was wanted by Interpol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is the end of your testimony, and you are now released as a witness. We will adjourn a little bit early -- or just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, Mr. Stringer, I think your application to have those two documents admitted is still alive? Okay. The documents are admitted and marked for the purposes mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 04974.09B will be Exhibit P3243. And document 04974.08F will be Exhibit P3244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, are they under seal or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Both. Both under seal, please. We'll take -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would inform the Chamber about one problem we met as to the witness schedule for the week of 8 and the week of 15 of September. And I don't know, is it appropriate time to do it right now or to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- or to wait --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Zivanovic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we plan for the week of 15 September, we planned to bring here DGH-046 and in our estimate he would take the whole week. However, on 26 of August, we were informed that the witness was sent to serve his sentence in another country. We tried to replace him with DGH-009 and we submit this request. We informed -- on 2nd of September, we informed Victims and Witness Section about it and asked to organise his travel for 10 of September. In addition, we asked for -- to another witness. They are DGH-099 and DGH-034 to organise their travel for 7 or 8 September, and such request was on 28th of August. For all of these witnesses we ask the safe conduct, safe conduct, so we are informed yesterday by the witness and victims section that even if we get the safe conduct -- conduct for these three witnesses they will not be able to organise their travel as planned. So we -- we'll try to -- to -- to fill this gap for the week of 8 of September. We have two or three witnesses for this week, for that week, but we -- we don't know whether we'll be able to -- to provide witnesses who do not ask -- who did not ask either safe conduct or videolink testimony. So I just like to inform the Chamber about this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that for next week, you have three witnesses without any specific measures asked for, or do you have no witnesses at all for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We hope we'll have the witnesses for next week. We have, I think, one viva voce witness. We have one witness for whom the protective measures and safe conduct was provided by the Chamber, and it seems that one of the witnesses planned for this week will stay the next week too. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will have the next week covered, so to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But the week after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the week -- our problem is with the week and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just I'd like to correct the transcript because it seems I -- I erroneously mentioned witness DGH-039 -- 34, sorry. It should be DGH-035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This reminds me of the request, the Prosecution's request yesterday about the protective measures decision. It is -- that decision forthcoming and is being prioritised by the Tribunal. We take a 30-minutes' break now, and we'll be back at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we heard you had another matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to answer on the Prosecution's request submitted yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- concerning disclosure of identity of two Defence witnesses. Namely, we'll today disclose the identity of DGH-047 through -- through the confidential written notice. And as for DGH-105, we would not yet disclose -- yet disclose his identity until we provide the permission of the competent authorities of Serbia for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We appreciate counsel's representation on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, just one moment. Just one moment, please. Mr. Hadzic, you have a problem with --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to deal with that. Do you get interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Hadzic now in the interpreters' booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, he said: Okay, thank you. In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm receiving interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So now everything is in order. Mr. Stringer, could you repeat your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to say thank you on the disclosure forthcoming on DGH-047. As for DGH-105, based on what counsel said, it sounds as though there is some sort of a Rule 70 type of impediment to disclosing his identity and we, of course, accept that. If that's the case. And we would expect that the timing of the witness's testimony in -- in terms -- in relation to the timing of the disclosure of his identity and statement will be regulated in the forthcoming protective measures decision. We're just concerned about having sufficient time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll take that into account, Mr. Stringer. Thank you. The next witness will be brought in. Mr. Gosnell, you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, or -- yes, good morning, Your Honour. Just to formally put on record that the Defence calls Amanda Celar as the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Mr. President, just while the witness is being brought in perhaps I could address a housekeeping matter in relation to the witness's statement. At present, the document that is uploaded under the 65 ter number for the witness's 92 ter statement is -- contains the annexes to that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in addition to the statement itself and some of those annexes have been admitted, and some -- at least provisionally, and some have not. And, in any event, it would be best if all of those documents are separated from the statement itself. So just to advise Your Honour that we do propose to just have the 30 pages of the statement as the -- as the document uploaded at the relevant number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Madam Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Trial Chamber. If I'm well-informed, you are an English speaker, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Amanda Celar and I was born on 7th of March, 1944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Please read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Gosnell, I take it you are leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Celar.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D3607, please. Ms. Celar, do you recognise the document on the right side of the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that your signature --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- down at the bottom right of the page?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page 30. Is that, again, your signature?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you recognise these two pages being the first and last page of a statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please move to page 26 of this document. Just there at the beginning of paragraph 81, is there a correction that you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes. The opening phrase, I would change to: "It's important to understand regarding the whole atmosphere and situation at that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And with that correction, is this statement true and accurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And does it reflect, in substance, what you would say if questioned on the same subjects?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, we would tender for admission 1D3607 and I would specify the first 30 pages of that document, thus, excluding all of the annexes that are currently appended to it, but then we would separately tender as well the six documents that were provisionally admitted to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 28 August 2014. And, if necessary, for the record I can read those 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would it be helpful to have them read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. I am standing to let the Court know that we are objecting to 1D3608. I know that the Trial Chamber issued its decision finding that the document was relevant and probative. We, however, think that that letter should be redacted to reflect the portions that are discussed in the witness's statement. So we would object to the admission of -- that's tab 9, 1D03608, and the Prosecution would not object to a redacted version of that, that only covers the portions discussed in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, could you eventually agree that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is the first notice I have of this objection, Mr. President, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall we MFI it for the moment and wait for, eventually, an agreement between parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in principle I would -- I would ask that it be admitted in the first instance because there is a -- already a Trial Chamber decision addressing the admission of this document and it has been litigated. So I would suggest that if there is now an objection being brought, it's a matter of reconsideration, and the admitted exhibit can be modified in accordance with any decision by the Trial Chamber or subsequent agreement by the parties. But, at the moment, I think it should be admitted in line with the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's a fair point and I understand the argument. What we discussed in our opposition, in our 92 ter response in this case, we said that it didn't -- it wasn't appropriate for admission. The Trial Chamber found that it was an integral part and it was relevant and probative. Based on that decision that was issued not very long ago, we believe that the entire document should not be admitted in its entirety because the basis for the Trial Chamber's agreement that it's appropriate as an associate exhibit said that: "It clarifies DGH-083's account of events in Osijek and makes positive reference to the letter in her written statement." So the Trial Chamber specifically pointed out to what the witness referred to in her statement as the basis for finding that it was relevant and probative, and so we're now asking that the version that's admitted be limited to those portions referenced by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As such, Ms. Biersay, the objection is overruled. As Mr. Gosnell says, you could eventually file a reconsideration motion but as an objection against something that has been decided, the objection is overruled. So the document is -- the documents are admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness statement document 1D3607 receives number D173. And Your Honours [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you hear me now. I repeat, the document 1D3607 will receive exhibit number D173. And we would kindly request Defence counsel to re-upload the 30 pages as tendered and admitted and notified so that the number can be assigned. The next document, 1D3365 will be Exhibit D174.173. Document number 1D3366 will be Exhibit D175.173. Document number 1D3367 will be Exhibit D176.173. Document 1D3368 will be Exhibit D177.173. Document 1D3608 will be Exhibit D178.173. And document number 1D3609 will be Exhibit D179.173. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have copies of the witness's statement that has just been admitted. I would request, since I will be referring to a couple of documents during my examination that will be pulled up on the screen and thereby displace her statement that Mrs. Celar be given a copy so she has it to hand, if I ask her to refer to it, or if she asks to refer to it, and I also have copies for Your Honours, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell, if you have them, it's always helpful to have them at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please turn to page 18 of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- which, Mrs. Celar, is your statement. And about three lines down in that page, which is the continuation of paragraph 52, you say: "I spoke with many of these refugees as I was involved in distributing humanitarian assistance in Baranja." And just to situate you, this is during the time-period following January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your daily activities during 1992 under the rubric of humanitarian assistance. What did that entail?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: First of all, we asked -- we were tasked with asking friends if they could spare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's -- could you hold it for a moment, Mrs. Celar, there is a problem with your microphone. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some days, not every day, we would meet friends and people we knew to ask them if they could spare something from their house, objects, like a cup, a plate, knives and forks. So that any newly arrived refugees could be given some of the minimum items if -- that they lacked. We would also go and try and greet newly arrived people, greet them simply really with a coffee and there wasn't a lot to give them. If we could give them some flour or -- this in the very early days, the Red Cross wasn't organised then very well to provide them with food. So we used to collect and give out what we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by 1992, approximately how long had you been living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, it's from -- do you mean in Osijek or do you mean in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in -- in Croatia generally?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: In Croatia generally that was from 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you are a native English speaker --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us how good or bad your Serbian was in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I would have said it was only reasonable. I could understand basic conversations, and then sometimes some of them spoke English, so we used a mixture of -- of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You anticipated my -- my next question, which is how it was that you communicated with the -- the refugees whom you were assisting, whether you -- you used, in general, Serbian, or did they speak English, or did you have interpretation of some sort?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I can't really be specific because I can't actually remember, but it was a mixture of all that. Sometimes I understood them. I could certainly understand people in distress. I was usually accompanied by somebody who spoke English and Serbian because they were -- I had close friends like that. Usually -- sometimes it was translated for me. Sometimes it didn't need translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you say that -- how frequent would you say were your contacts with refugees, let's say, during the -- the year 1992 as a whole?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, it was very often -- very frequent. Early in 1992, before the attacks, it was daily. And then after it was probably less, but I saw of them frequently, really, because we -- we befriended a lot of them but the one who were in Beli Manastir not the ones who were in the villages around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you've just referred to attacks. Which attacks are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I'm talking about particularly the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Right now, if we could look at paragraph 53 of your statement. You say: "Most of the refugees told me that they had come from other parts of Croatia, more specifically, the areas bordering on the Baranja, the Knin area, Western Slavonia, and the Vukovar area... the refugees to Baranja from Knin and Western Slavonia would have had to pass through Bosnia and Serbia."

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if I can just ask you for one point of clarification on that. Did the refugees explain to you whether they had travelled continuously from Western Slavonia and Knin, in a single journey or did they mention whether they had stopped and stayed for any interval of time in Serbia before moving on to Baranja?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that I ever had a conversation regarding that. Not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did any describe whether they had stayed in -- for any period in Serbia before coming to Baranja?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No. My impression was that because they came with nothing a lot of them, carrier bags, I suppose I assumed they came straight to Baranja, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did the refugees tell you or express how they expected they would remain or stay in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No. The overwhelming sense I got from them was that they were pleased to be in a place of safety but they were so shocked. It was hard to -- they didn't really have normal conversations in those early days. It was later on, after they'd been there for a while, that they would wanted to talk about where they wanted to go or if they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Where did they say they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And home for them was the places from which they had originated --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if I can just continue with paragraph 53. "Their desire to come to Baranja as opposed to Serbia, for example, may have been a result of family relations or a desire to stay as close as possible to the places from which they had fled. They were from Croatia, after all, and it would be normal to want to stay in Croatia - just as Ilija and I did." And then down at paragraph 55, related to this: "I never heard that these refugees were bussed in as part of a policy to displace Croats." And then further along in paragraph 55, page 18 over to page 19, you say: "Some refugees came for one or two months and would then leave as soon as they found somewhere to go in Serbia." Now, where -- what do you mean when you say "found somewhere to go in Serbia"? Where could or would they find to go in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, a lot -- they -- they didn't want to go and join -- go to a camp in Serbia, so they were trying to find a job somewhere where they thought perhaps there would be housing or family members that could take them in. But the situation in Serbia was very difficult because of -- I think the embargo had made the economic climate there pretty desperate, and so that's what they were searching for, somewhere to be permanent, I think. I don't think they regarded Baranja as permanent because the climate was awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was your impression from speaking to refugees that they considered they were welcomed in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, they didn't feel welcome in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you've referred to camps. Do you know anything about these camps? Did any of them describe to you the conditions in the camps that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I just heard that there were camps in Serbia for displaced people and that they weren't very comfortable or -- I didn't know anything about the camps, really, only odd bits of things I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it your impression that the refugees that you did speak to about the camps considered those conditions to be less favourable than those they found in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have P2400, which is Defence tab 16. Now, Mrs. Celar, at various points in your statement you describe biased media coverage of events in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in particular, by western media sources. And I'd now like to look together with you, please, at one example of western media coverage of events in Baranja, in particular --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, I can't really read this. It's far away from me. Can it be magnified?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Any possibility we can blow up the English version a little more?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that better, Mrs. Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go through some portions of this news report from The Independent newspaper, dated 27 September 1992. Can I first ask you, were you in Baranja at this time?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 seems to refer to a conversation with Borivoje Zivanovic, who is described here as the self-styled mayor of Beli Manastir, who is reported as "predicts a 1.000-year Serbian Reich in Baranja and is helping to create what appears to be a hermetically sealed state under the impotent gaze of UN peacekeepers." And if we can now skip to page three of this document, please. At the very top of the page there, which is now being zoomed in, the first paragraph: "The imported Serbs are not allowed to leave Baranja, even to visit Serbia in case they jump ship. Only Croats and Hungarians are allowed out of the enclave." Now, first of all, is it true that Serbs were not permitted to leave Baranja --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was the procedure for leaving, if you were a Serb?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was the same procedure for everybody, including me, and I had to go to the opstina and get a document about leaving, and it would be stamped. And then I'd show that at Batina, and I could leave. And when I came back in, I had to re-register at the opstina and have my paper stamped that I could be there. But everybody did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were -- were such permissions granted --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in practice?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we can go back to page 1, please, of this document there's this reference in this language of predicting a 1.000-year Serbian Reich in Baranja. Do you think it's plausible that Mr. Zivanovic would have used that particular language?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's plausible at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Because he wasn't that sort of person. I knew him and he was really trying to establish some sort of order and normal life for people in -- certainly, in Beli Manastir. I was only ever really in Beli Manastir at this time, so I don't know about the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is the reference to a "Reich" something that in your experience would have been likely for someone of a --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't believe he would have ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we could look down at paragraph 4 of this -- this page. It says: "More than 50 Hungarians and Croats have been murdered in recent weeks." Now this is a document dated the 27th of September. Can I ask you whether you heard whether there were any murders on this scale. Here it says 50 Hungarians and Croats. Were there any murders on that scale occurring during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I never heard of any such murders. Can I also say that Mr. Zivanovic used my husband as an interpreter, because he was one of the few that was well versed in Serbian and English languages, and he always translated for him. So that -- on reflection, the conversation with Mr. Zivanovic, I'm sure he would have called my husband to translate because we didn't have any reporters there. Only one. Only one other reporter came at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The article continues: "Almost every Croatian church in the region has been blown up." Now, is -- is that true, to your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, it's not. And Jack Klein attended some church services in the village of Suza and some of the other villages, Hungarian villages, there in late 1994, 1995. And other UN personnel had attended -- they were either Calvinist services or Catholic services. They weren't the Serbian churches and those church services were being held all during that time and the priest there, the Catholic or the Calvinist priest because my husband attended and acted as translator for those services. The two churches I knew that were blown up was one in -- well, they weren't blown up, they were burnt down actually. It was arson. The one in Jagodnjak -- no, sorry, Ceminac, and the one in Beli Manastir. Because when the -- particularly the one in Beli Manastir, because when it was set fire to, alarms went out and people ran up there, including my husband and he managed to take out the Bible and the priest's mantle and other things from the altar and he brought them home. Although I'm a Protestant, not a Catholic, I looked after them until 1996 and just before we left, I handed them to the -- a family I referred to later Rakajic [phoen] family, for them to return to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The document or this article says that no Catholic priests are tolerated. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, no, they left. But the Serbian priests had all come from Croatia and the Catholic priests, as far I know went back but. There was never any discussion about not tolerated them. In fact, in -- when my father died in June 1991, I went to the Catholic priest in Ceminac to ask him if I could talk to him about the death of my father, but he didn't invite me in so I eventually went to find the Orthodox priest. I felt I needed to talk to a priest at that time. That was in June that my father died, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we can turn over to page 2 of this article, third paragraph down, which is in the middle of the page, there's a quote attributed to someone named Blandina Negga: "Ms. Negga described the level of terrorism in UN zones as very high, adding that 99 per cent of the victims are non-Serbs." Now, we don't know what she may mean by terrorism, but is it true that 99 per cent of the victims of crime were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I would say that the wrong word is being used there. There was a high level of criminality. I was a victim. I lost my camera, which was in the -- one of the repair shops which was raided and everything taken. And on a smaller level, when all the women were alone at night, if their husbands were on the front line, we locked ourselves in and I had all my livestock stolen one night. And others had their livestock stolen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Ms. Negga," the article continues, "linked the rise in terrorism to the bussing into Baranja mainly by night of thousands of Serbian refugees from Bosnia and other parts of Croatia. The import of Bosnian Serbs at the request of the local Serbian authorities cannot be stopped by the UN." Are you aware whether any of the refugees with whom you came in contact were Bosnian Serbs instead of being from other parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I personally never met anybody who said they'd come from Bosnia as a refugee. And the only buses I was ever aware of were when they brought back the women and children, all the women and children of Baranja area, in -- in May 1991. They took all the -- those that wanted to go, women and children, were evacuated to Serbia to Prigorica [phoen] I think it was called, and after September 1991 when some sort of order had been restored they brought them back in those and there were many hundreds of women and children brought back. But they were the people who lived there and were returning to their homes because the fighting had stopped then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were those buses coming into Baranja at night?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Nobody would have been able to come to Baranja at night because they closed the bridge. There was a curfew. It was extremely dangerous to come from Batina bridge from Knezevi Vinogradi towards Beli Manastir and on one occasion when I was in an UN vehicle being taken to somewhere, they told me to lie down in the back seat and that was in the afternoon because of snipers along the road. It was dangerous. But the town itself at night was just pitch black. Nobody went out and it was as quiet as you could imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why didn't people go out?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: They were frightened, really. There were incursions. There was fear, even if they weren't actually -- because most of the men were gone at night onto the front lines and the women stayed in because they were afraid to go out. Even the old men were formed into some sort of small bands, and they went out and guarded the water installation which was in the fields along -- near where we were living. And they went to protect that. And then, of course, the shelling would start in the evening, so, all together, it was better -- we usually -- if shelling wasn't there, we stayed in. We'd open windows to talk to each other across the street and if the shelling had started then we'd quickly run to the basement -- if you didn't have a basement, you had to go to a neighbour's basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D3367, please, Defence tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just to situate ourselves in your statement, you describe the arrival of UNPROFOR, starting at paragraph 70 onwards. And I would, in particular, direct your attention to paragraph 74, which is relevant to this document. And this document appears to be a code cable from Goulding to Nambiar dated 23rd of March, 1992. And it reads: "Please find attached cable received at headquarters today from Ms. Amanda Brook, an English woman married to a Serb and resident in Beli Manastir who has corresponded in the past with us. Please advise whether this allegation accords with information you have on continuing cease-fire violations in that area." Now before we turn over to look at the correspondence in question, can I ask you whether you know what previous correspondence appears to be referred to in this code cable?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I don't have any personal recollection of personally corresponding with them. I would suppose it might have come from the reports I was sending to Ian Greer in London organisation, and they were... But I don't have any recollection of talking to the UN before this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we go over to page 2, please. Now I won't, Mrs. Celar, attempt to read this verbatim because there are some spelling errors but I think the gist is clear for all of us to see without having to read it. Can I just ask you what circumstances led you to right this particular cable.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: There was tremendous fear at that time amongst everyone because the shelling had intensified into the town, and my husband, amongst others that were patrolling along the banks of the Drava came back and said to me that they were massing there, they thought Croatian forces were massing there, had lots of boats ready to come across the river Drava. And that they expected an attack, a full attack. There had been small incursions where some of the soldiers on the front line had been killed, and he said to me, Can you please see if can you do anything? They were waiting for the implementation of something from the UN so I can't remember the number, implement 743, as referred to here. So we thought if they implemented that at the United Nations then the UN forces would be able to come out from behind all these barricades they'd built and were behind in Beli Manastir. And we were very afraid that there would be a big attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, these UN forces that you have just referred to and you have implicitly answered my question but were they already there at this time, were they present?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes they had been there -- if I recall from around 16th August but nobody knew quite what they were doing there. Because they took over the army, the Yugoslav army dog training barracks. Once they all left then the UN came and they built a lot of sandbag emplacements around the front of the -- there was a lot of buildings there it was a complex and they sat behind them and, at first, people just looked at them and, later on, started to ignore them because they -- we -- nobody knew quite what they were doing there. We supposed they were waiting for this mandate to be implemented, but the fear amongst the population was that -- the suspicion was that they were waiting for the Croats to attack. Because it was perfectly obvious to everyone that something was going to happen and they were waiting to see if the Croats would be successful before intervening. This was what was a strongly held view by the people I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How far was that dog training centre that you referred to from your house, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Maybe 2 kilometres. It was at the beginning of the entrance to the town of Beli Manastir, on the road leading into the town itself. So I'm not very good with distances. Maybe 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And to try to pin down the date more accurately, can you situate in time how long before you sent this telegram did UN forces arrive?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, they had already arrived. I said they were there but I didn't feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sure, Mrs. Celar, if I can just intervene. I understand they were already there but can you remember how long before you sent this cable had they arrived?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: They had been there from about the 16th of the month, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by the month, you mean the month of March?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes. But that's when we noticed them. I don't know how long before they -- I don't know whether there were people that came before they actually established themselves there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And rather than sending a cable to Shashi Tharoor, why didn't you simply go to their base and convey this particular information to them?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I didn't feel -- we felt that they were not actually very supportive of the situation and we felt they were on the side of the Croatian people and that they weren't very interested in -- this is just an impression. I have absolutely no basis for saying that but that was the opinion of all the people, that they were all waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 76 of your statement, you describe having a meeting with some representatives of the Belgian Battalion who apparently, according to you are -- or have been sent in response to this particular cable that you've sent. And you said: "I told them that the only way that they could be ignorant of the fighting was if they were not engaging in any patrolling." Now did -- and this is not mentioned in your statement, but did they, Mr. Malherbe or anyone else, part of this group that came to see you, did they say anything about whether they were or were not patrolling in response to your complaint?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: They said -- there was a conversation that went something like this. He said, Why did you send that cable? I said, Because everybody is afraid of an imminent attack and there are incursions already happening. And he said, We have no record of any incursions or any fighting. And I said, Well, you wouldn't because you're not there on the front line checking what's happening. You can't see anything when you're all behind your bunkers at the top of Beli Manastir. And he said, We have no mandate to do any patrolling. We're not allowed to go and patrol. So I said, If you don't go and patrol there, you won't see any fighting. They're not doing it in the town, it's on the River Drava.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On paragraph 74 of your statement and I suppose now we can pull that up on the screens please. Now, that's D173, page 24, and you describe that there was an infantry attack that occurred on the 3rd of April, 1992, and you say: "Infantry came across the Drava, and tanks crossed the Hungarian border in support of the attack, from what I heard. Do you know whether the UN forces present there did anything in response to this attack?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, I -- no. We collected in the -- we -- we were called about 4.00 in the afternoon to go and watch the lorries coming back from the front line to -- really to go and see if your husband or son, whatever, were with -- they brought the wounded back, and it was very much a Serbian -- I didn't see any UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever subsequently hear that they did anything in response to this attack --
