utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what was the ethnicity of those who were working for the UN forces based in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: The -- the people who were working within the BelBat complex were all Croatians, from Croatia, and most of the Serbs that were working as interpreters and staff, including my husband, after that mandate was implemented, were -- they were working for CIVPOL as translators and support staff. But that was for CIVPOL, not for the BelBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can look at the middle of paragraph 77 of your statement, you are describing a meeting with some Belgian officers who are part of BelBat and the JNA commander in the area, Mr. Krstic. And you report here that Colonel -- or that Mr. Malherbe said: "You don't understand, Amanda, these people are not civilised like us. They don't behave the same way we do." Can you tell us for clarity what you understood him to mean when he said "these people"? Who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, he is referring to the Serbs that were in the area where they were acting. And the impression I got was the way I would imagine as if they were colonialists that were treating with the local inhabitants. He was very dismissive. Actually, I got very angry with him and I did say I am appalled that they can ap point people as ignorant as you are of the culture, how old the Serbian culture is. And then I childishly said to him, Whereas Belgium is only about 200 years old how can you make such a distinction about Serbs? It was ignorance. I was so angry because he assumed that nobody else in the room spoke English, which I understood they did they afterwards, but they didn't choose to at the time. And I was embarrassed that they could hear this sort of conversation. I thought it was dreadful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who you characterise generally between BelBat and the local population in Beli Manastir as you observed it, or heard about it?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was very poor. It wasn't friendly. I didn't hear of people -- I heard of people being offended by the way they presented themselves. They tended to swagger, do a lot of swaggering about and all the more noticeable because it was so different with the Pakistani Battalion in Darda and later CIVPOL, who everybody got quite friendly with. In a -- not in a bad way. Respected each other, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was any sentiment locally about whether BelBat should be replaced by a contingent of a different nationality?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, they didn't want -- they thought BelBat were on the side of Croatians. They had no -- that was the impression of the populace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you think it was justified that there was that wish to replace them?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: If it would have helped the situation I think it would have been far better. Because there is always a certain amount of paranoia in a situation like that. But it certainly didn't help to bring a feeling of any sort of security for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Celar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. President, no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment to reorganise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I -- I look at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I greet you. Good afternoon, Mrs. Celar.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My name is Lisa Biersay. We haven't met, and I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I have been granted three hours to ask you questions, that time may be shorter, or I may request a longer time. It all depends on how efficient we are with questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly observe pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mrs. Celar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, there's no problem. It's just to let you know that when people are speaking the same language, there's still need for translation and interpretation, and the interpreters, of course, need time to do that. So if we can avoid overlap between questions and answers that would be very nice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's likely it was meant for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: From reading your materials and listening to you, you talk a lot about your husband, Ilija Celar --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have the sense that you and Ilija Celar have a very tight bond?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, we have a wonderful marriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you've been married for how many years at this point?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, we were partners at first and then married, but 27 years in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And from what I gathered from the materials, it was love at first sight that has endured time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, in fact, the Netherlands is a special place for the two of you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Because that's where you met?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We met in Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he also come with you on this trip to the --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Netherlands? And why not? Why didn't he come?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We have a farm and there's nobody else to take care of the livestock and I also rescue dogs and nobody will volunteer to look after seven dogs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now back in 1987, it was because of your love for Ilija Celar that you moved to a new country. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We discussed where we'd both like to live actually. And he was due to go to South Africa and I didn't want to go to South Africa. He didn't want to live in England. We found Amsterdam too expensive and we thought the then-Yugoslavia would be a lovely place to live.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So again, because of your relationship, that why you --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yeah, mutual decision to go somewhere nice to live together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And because of that bond you took on the challenge of learning a new language --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, and also because I teach English there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And learning a new culture?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you had to learn a very complicated and long history of the region and all the people there.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I didn't have to. When we first moved there, it was Yugoslavia and I wasn't aware at all of different ethnic groups. I just wasn't aware of it at first because there were -- there is a lot of intermarriage there, tremendous amounts of intermarriage. So my brother-in-law was Croatian and his wife was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say that when you moved there you weren't aware of all the different ethnic groups how did you come to learn about the different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, if you listened to people talking and some of the people wanted to talk to me because I was English and there weren't many English people living there, if any. I don't think there were any and they wanted to tell me their history. They were very proud of their history but it was usually about Yugoslavia and about Tito, because there was still Communism when I first went there but a very easy -- a very easy form of Communism.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you learned the language, the culture, the history, mostly through your interactions with Ilija Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Not the language, because he insists on speaking English all the time because he wants to perfect his language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So your home language was --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Was English --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And I learned more English -- I was very lazy. Everybody I met wanted to speak English to practice their English. So for a long time I didn't learn as much as I could have done. But I actually learnt it from girlfriends that didn't speak English that I -- taught me or neighbours, I was drinking coffee with. It was a very sociable society.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the language you learned from other people, and the history and the culture and all of that, you learned mostly from Ilija Celar.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I read. I'm a -- I'm an independent person. Ilija discussed what happened on Kosovo and things like that, but he didn't particularly -- he taught me some of it or if I asked questions but I asked other people. I didn't just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'm just looking at the clock but I think we'll have enough time to start this segment. I would like some help in understanding the timeline of where you lived in the former Yugoslavia. So when you first arrived in 1987, you lived with Ilija Celar's mother in Jagodnjak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes. And also, at the same time, we stayed with his sister in Ceminac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In Ceminac?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We stayed in both places at some point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have stable home in Jagodnjak did you stay there for a certain period of time --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Or you --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We stayed between the two places and they've got families and they didn't really have very big houses. We stayed really until we managed to find a property in Osijek, which is what we were looking for, to go and live in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when did you make the move to Osijek?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I think it was in early -- early 1988. After the Serbian Christmas, which is in January. So I think it was -- could have been February. I can't precisely remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sounds like Jagodnjak and Osijek are two very different types of places, like one is very big compared to the other?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, Osijek is the town over the river, a regional town, big town, and Jagodnjak and Ceminac are in Baranja, in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you get to know Jagodnjak and the people there even though --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Later on, I did, but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say later on, when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: After we left Osijek in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it's after you left Osijek that you learned, really, the people and the town of Jagodnjak. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And Ceminac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Ceminac.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Because we had a flat in Jagodnjak that belonged to Ilija's brother who was a doctor in Germany and didn't use it and he let us use the flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where was that apartment?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Near the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time, Your Honours, would this would be a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry to raise this. I don't have an exhibit list yet from the Prosecution. Maybe there won't be any exhibits used.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No. It should have been released about ten minutes ago. I'll check it. But we'll take care of it during the break. Thank you for raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like just to go back to our conversation about Jagodnjak. You described that you were living in a flat that was near the medical centre. Was that an apartment building or a house? What was it?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was flat that was given to the doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you get a little closer to the --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's not picking up. There you go.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was the flat that belonged to the medical centre which -- Ilija's brother was the appointed doctor for that medical centre although he was in --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sorry to --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: -- Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- interrupt. Just to describe what kind of structure it was?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was a single story building. The medical centre was on the left and the flat was on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was single story but just split into two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So after you moved to Osijek, you continued to travel to Jagodnjak, I would imagine, to visit --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ilija Celar's --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And Ceminac, for family. And also, I can`t remember the name of the other little town there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we remind you not to overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How frequently would you make the trip from Osijek to Jagodnjak, say, in a week?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I -- it would depend on what was happening. And it was a two- or three-year period, so it depended if there was a family Slava or celebration or wedding or just to see them socially. I think we used to go there most Sundays for lunch because they worked all during the week, so it was probably weekends we went, unless there was a holiday or a celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so for what time-period did you live in Osijek total?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1988 until when we left in April, I think it was April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go after you and Ilija Celar left Osijek?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, we went to that flat in Jagodnjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Got it. When -- how long did you stay in that flat?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I stayed there until June, the 17th. And then my father died, so within a couple of days I travelled back to England. And I didn't see the flat again until probably the next year to go and retrieve some of my possessions. The first time it was safe to go back there. I didn't live in it again after that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which flat are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Jagodnjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you start living in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: When I came back from England. October, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did you find the house or the place where you lived in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I went -- I was escorted from the bridge in Batina. I'd had a call from a -- I'd had a call from a journalist that Ilija had been wounded and Ilija had given him a message to try and get the message to me. So this journalist rang me at my home in England and that's why I came back in October, I think, and I came to the bridge, but I didn't -- I didn't have any sort of paperwork. So they took me from the Batina bridge, straight to the police station in Beli Manastir. And then when they found out who I was, one of the wives of one of the people in Ilija's group, came and took me to her house for a few days, and then they said that there was another house that -- they'd put all the special forces fighters in one district of the -- of this -- of Beli Manastir so that if they -- when they had an alarm because there weren't that many of them they could find them and they could respond to the alarm. So I didn't find out actually where I was going to live and I didn't live in it until after January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So where did you live between October 1991 and January 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly reminded to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the reminder. I will be more mindful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived with Ilija's nephew and niece who were living in their aunt's house in Beli Manastir. Their aunt was Croatian and had gone to Croatia, and this is where the father is Croatian and their mother is Serbian. And they'd stayed in Serbia. So they were living in the aunt's house and I stayed with them until Ilija came out of hospital, I think. Until Ilija came out of hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to back up just a little bit from October 1991 to January 1992, you lived with family --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where in Beli Manastir was that?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: In -- I can't remember the name of the street. It was where the other house was, where we moved into when Ilija came out of hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So in January 1992, you moved into a house in Beli Manastir where you would stay for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you find the house that you --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I didn't find it. I just moved into it. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me just finish my question. We will help each other and the translators and the interpreters as well. How did you and Ilija Celar come to live in the place where you moved in January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I only knew -- that was where I was told was where we were going to live. And that the special forces because the whole street had about five or six other people that were in the special forces that were living there as well, including -- it was the house next door to the house that Ilija's niece and nephew were living in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of -- that street?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Truthfully, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll ask you another question in the meantime. Is it fair to say that when you were actually in the former Yugoslavia from 1987 to 1993, you lived in Jagodnjak, sometimes Ceminac, Osijek, or Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What period of time was Ilija Celar in hospital? You said that it was after he came out of hospital that you moved to this permanent -- more permanent address in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, he must have come back in the October because I went back to Britain, I'm sorry, I'm getting confused. It was in October that we moved into this -- I stayed with these -- until he came out of hospital. He came out of hospital at the -- sometime before I went back to Britain which would have been November. I'm not absolutely clear of that period, because it was very traumatic. My father had just died and Ilija had been injured and my journey from the airport to Baranja was dreadful. I think we moved into that place in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What you just described as a very traumatic period of time from June until the end of 1991 for you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Until November. And then I went back to England, because it was so dangerous, there was so much shelling, Ilija really didn't want me to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you and Ilija Celar became politically involved, politically active?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No. I have never been politically active.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you or Ilija Celar support the SDS, which is very popular then in Jagodnjak in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I don't know whether Ilija did, but I had nothing do with politics at all. I've always regarded myself, and I still do, as a guest in the country and as such I've never got involved with politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You referred to yourself as a guest in the country and I'm -- I recall having read somewhere where you described yourself as a Serbophile?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I am. I love Serbs. I didn't mean to say I think I'm a Serb. I'm not. I shall always be English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So are you saying that do not know, whether Ilija Celar supported the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he did. But he doesn't vote. He is not a very political person. But I can say that he is a nationalist if that means he was of that party. He hasn't got a very good opinion of politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you would describe him as a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just quickly, regarding the special forces fighters who were living in this district, that house that you lived in, in the end of 1991 to 1992, who were they? Who are these special forces fighters that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, if you understand that the first 18, was started -- when the fighting started on August the 19th in Beli Manastir, there were a group of 19 who met to discuss how they were going do defend themselves because they felt under attack and they were the core, that when they were attacked by the Croatian police, that was the first -- that was the beginning of the fighting in Beli Manastir and others came to join them, I think in total -- some of them got killed. There were about 46 of them and there were very few of them. And they then, as I say in here, that the Croatians thought there were far more of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It's all to do with that and it's all those -- the ones who formed themselves into a defensive group, I would say. It wasn't a political group. It was a defensive group.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. And Ilija Celar was a member of this special forces fighters.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you describe hearing the slogan "Croatia for Croats" during the 1990 election campaign?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in response to some questions asked by Mr. Gosnell, you explained that by the end of 1992 your Serbian was reasonable?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I wondered where were you hearing these slogans? TV?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: TV -- well, we used to watch Croatian television, always, because they had far better programs on than Serbian television. And I would see various news items or a few things impressed me that I didn't like with the -- not exactly your question, but when they had church services they'd got Croatian flag around the candles which I thought was offensive. There were a few things that I didn't -- but that was nothing to do with -- I didn't discuss it with anybody. It's just I was watching what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. It will be important for each of us to track each other as far as questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: All right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just to be a little more concise.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So my question to you was regarding the slogans you were hearing and given the challenges you had with the language, where were you hearing these slogans?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, this wasn't a difficult slogan to understand. Hrvatska za Hrvate, I knew what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have another --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: We had friends that -- when we went there initially, it was Yugoslavia. Everybody -- I didn't hear any ethnicity that's why I -- this came as a slow process. I can't say it suddenly happened. It just came in, insidiously, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where else would you get your information about current affairs? Croatian TV, is that the only place?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Croatian television. Well, friends. We had a lot of friends that came and visited us. A lot of them spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And they would tell you, keep you abreast of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, it depended which perspective they were coming from. We had all sorts of friends. We didn't limit ourselves to Serbian friends. We had Croatian friends. As I said, there were so many mixed marriage friends. One of my most dear friend is a Muslim. It came from very different sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Those source would say include the media, your friends, your partner, Ilija Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Could have. Yes, I would certainly know his opinion on things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you also describe how rhetoric about Croatia's Fascist past. I think what you say is that it provoked genuine and extreme fear amongst Serbs living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, are you saying that Serbs became fearful because of what they heard Croatian politicians saying?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It was more than that. It was the flag. It was the uniforms. And it was this statement that they'd got to sign in order to stay at their place of work, the contract, because they were all replicas of what had been used during that independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you know about the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I'd known it because I studied previously the history of World War II. I also met Michael Lees, who worked with the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say worked with the Chetniks you actually served --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: During the Second World War, he was with the Chetniks. And I didn't necessarily agree with him because he was -- he was a royalist, and didn't have a good word to say about Tito, really. Whereas lots of people did have nice things to say about Tito. It was -- my conception of what the country would be like wasn't anything what it was like in reality when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. One of the events that made Serbs more fearful would be the discussion about Croatia's Fascist past; right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also mentioned that talk about the past genocide against the Serb people also triggered fear in them, right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did it trigger fear in Ilija Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it as fear. He was deeply unhappy. Ilija was essentially, when I first knew him before the war began, a Yugoslav and a lot of our friends were perfectly satisfied with the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Celar. Just to back up one -- one minute. You said, I wouldn't describe it as fear. He was deeply unhappy; right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just ask you why wouldn't you describe that as -- as fear?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, it's not a -- it's not something I'd describe as -- as -- as -- a fear, because nobody believed there was going to be any fighting. Everybody said, It's only these leaders that are -- the rhetoric but people won't actually fight each other. We're related to each other. We're family. The big -- Croats came to our house. They didn't come as Croats; they came as friends and they would have an opinion about what was happening for independence for Croatia. We would have our opinion about it. We would talk about in those days or disagree with them. We had a visitor who had been a refugee in the Second World War, had -- and talked what she was going through. She was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No -- I'm sorry, it's just very complicated. It's not simplistic at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It`s not simplistic; is it?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So that's why I would ask you to listen to my questions and I apologise, because I will have to continue trying to bring you back to the question.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One of the things you talked about, you talked about the flag --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: That was explained to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, let me just finish the question. You described the flag being something that upset Serbs --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- right? You describe in your statement that the flag of Croatia in 1990/1991 was the exact same flag was used by the Fascists in the 1940s --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And my question to you is: What was the basis of that? Who told you that.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I just think it was a point of discussion that was brought up when we were talking about it. I don't recall anybody saying this is -- the start of the discussion about the flag and -- and this sort of thing was begun when we saw these black shirts in Osijek, when I was out shopping --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand the context --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And that led to us discussing whether the people, and with Ilija, and saying what's going on?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: -- and during those discussions --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Celar, one moment, please. My question to you is how did you get your information about the flags being the same and I believe you answered that. You said that people told you; right? Was Ilija Celar one of the people who told you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: He could have been. I can't categorically tell you who specifically at that time told me this sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Had you actually seen the flags?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you actually don't know if they're exactly the same, do you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, only by what I've read and heard, but I hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also referenced the pledge of allegiance as being something that instilled fear in Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you say that it was exactly the same language that had been used by the independent state of Croatia. What is the basis for --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It's the same thing. It was the discussion said that the flag, the insignia of the uniforms and -- it was the three things that the -- the paper that they had to sign of allegiance to Croatia were all replicas of what had been used in that government.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this is what you heard from Ilija Celar and others?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And others, when we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Celar, in your statement, you say that you did not hear rhetoric from the Serb side about Greater Serbia. You said that it arose later and had little appeal. Do you recall that from your statements?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I never really heard anybody talking about Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I never heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What does the phrase "Greater Serbia" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I would imagine that a Serbia that could expand borders and take over the countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the expansion of borders --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I would imagine so. That's what it would mean to me literally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you start hearing that kind of rhetoric?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I never heard that sort of rhetoric. I'm just answering what that would mean to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I heard Yugoslavia. At that time it was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So in 1991, 1992, you were not hearing Serbs talk about the adjustment of borders?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I was told that they were -- that there were other reasons -- yes. Okay. I heard about the adjustment of borders like this. That Baranja had never been Croatian and, therefore, it should never be Croatian territory and that Tito had drawn the borders as he saw fit and nobody challenged it. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Ultimately, I know borders were drawn at difference times. At that was at the time when you -- when people get together and put grievances together, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Apologies for the interruption, Mr. President, but what was put by my learned friend at page 78, line 1, you did not hear -- "In your statement you say that you did not hear rhetoric from the Serb side about Greater Serbia." That's not precisely what is in Mrs. Celar's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm happy to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I apologise for the delay in noting that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 5: "I would add that neither at this stage nor later did I hear any equivalent rhetoric from the Serb side concerning Greater Serbia." And Mrs. Celar answered my question. So now I'd like to ask you another question --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You talked about the expansion of borders and I wondered in what context did you hear that kind of discussion, about it -- Baranja never being Croatian, should never be Croatian territory, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: That was later. That was after the fighting began and we went to live in Baranja and that I heard my husband and others saying that they were really -- if -- an autonomous area is what they'd like. To be neither affiliated with -- if it couldn't be Yugoslavia, they didn't want to be part of Serbia and they didn't want to be part of Croatia. They thought about an autonomous area, like Luxembourg.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you heard that from Ilija Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you heard of Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would like to play tab 16 which is Exhibit 1726. And I will tell you that the information I have is this is April 1991, and it's Seselj in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Actually, if we could wait one minute before starting. I understand that we have a new protocol of checking with the booth to see whether or not the transcript is ready to go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And a very helpful one, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It has been proven to be very helpful, indeed. So I'm just awaiting confirmation from the booth that they have P1726.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so I'd like to go ahead and play this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Serbia, Serbia. Serbian people live here. This is Serbian land and it will remain Serbian forever. After calling the decision on the establishment of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina historical Seselj said, Serbian brothers and sisters, you find yourself in the front lines defending the Serbian cause. The Serbian state borders. You are in the most difficult position and you are the pride of the whole of Serbdom. He has promised them they would not left to themselves and that all the Serbs in Croatia have only one party, the Serbian Democratic Party. You have a wise and brave leadership headed by the heroic Dr. Milan Babic. Those who divide the Serbian people he labelled as traitors. Only Ante Markovic's mercenaries and those of foreign intelligence services believe today that there are more important problems that your defence, your protection. They offer you up to Tudjman. They would sell you. You will not be sold or betrayed. Instead of calming them down, Seselj sent a message to the gathered people as follows: We are sending a message to the new Ustasha head of state and Ustasha regime in Croatia. Serbian heads have rolled, struck down by the Ustasha hands in the Serbian Krajina, as Serbian head rolled in Serbian Western Srem and Slavonia as well. We will avenge Serbian blood. We will."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that rally in Plitvice was very well attended?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you heard when Seselj talked about defending the Serb cause and defending Serbian state borders?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear about that big rally and speech in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- in April --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: -- I may have seen it, but it didn't really concern me. I wasn't -- I mean I -- he was a politician. He has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear about the rally?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I can't say that I did. I may have done at the time but it's not something that stayed in my memory as important.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know that Seselj came to Jagodnjak to give a speech?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I heard -- yes, I heard he was there, and I know Ilija went to see him but I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did Ilija Celar tell you what was said at that rally?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I knew that he rallying the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me play for you tab 6, which is exhibit 240.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're checking the technical issue of the tab number, did you ever hear about the concept of distinguishing between Croats who were natives to Baranja versus others who had come after the war?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Which war do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The Second World War.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: After Second World War, my husband's family came from Bosnia. They were relocated there in 1948. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For Croats, did you hear that there was reference to Croats being brought in after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, because the Germans had all gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: But nobody differentiated between how many Croats came and how many Serbs came.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. So tab 7, exhibit 240 if I could get a confirmation from the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] This is a nice occasion so I will try to show you a historical fact. Croats who live here came to your fields and to your homes, Pavelic colonised them here because they were good butchers. They still live here to this day. The Hungarians here don't wish to be the same as those in Backa because they primarily serve Tudjman. This is Serbian land and they must realise that they are intruders and they will have to leave if they don't want to live nicely with us. They are perpetually trying to put us down, to destroy our borders and our graveyards. Hungarians must not dig up..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I paused it here where it is subtitled, "to destroy our borders and our graveyards," to ask you if you recognise anyone on the stage.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: The man on the right I have seen before but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On the right --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: On the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the front?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With the white shirt and the grey jacket.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, with the white --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And no -- no tie?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You recognise him --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you don't recall his name?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: And -- Seselj is there. I don't know who the speaker is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is Milan Paroski.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] ... Medieval archeological finds because all they will find are Serbs. Now they have stopped their archeological research. This is the truth so whoever comes and tells you that this is his land, he is a usurper. He has come to take the land and you have the right to kill him like a dog."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did Ilija Celar tell you that someone at the rally said that this -- anyone who asked for this land is a usurper and you have the right to kill him like a dog?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The Croats can leave Yugoslavia wherever they please, but they have to note that they cannot take a single foot of Serbian land with them, not a single acre that holds Serbian villages, churches, Serbian death pits, death camps, Serbian Jasenovac. If we were to allow that we would unworthy of our glorious ancestors, and we would have to feel ashamed before our descendants, the Croats may create their own state but only west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. That's right. Everything east of that line belongs to the Serbs and we shall not allow the Croats to manipulate the Serbs who are Bunjevci and the Serbs who are Sokci. They are Catholic Serbs and we hope that soon their eyes will be also be opened and that they will realise what role the Vatican and the Ustasha want them to play against the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You heard Seselj mention that Croats were free to have their own state but west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Had you heard that before?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Today is the first time you're hearing of this line from Seselj?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ilija Celar never talked to you about that line?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He didn't tell you that it was discussed at the rally that he attended?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No. Because there were lot of rallies and there were lots of things being said. That was before the war started and there were a lot of meetings he went to. I didn't -- we didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So when Ilija Celar went to these meetings --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't know where that line is anyway. I know where Vinkovci is, but I don't know what line you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps tomorrow I will bring a map so that can you see that it's west of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How frequently would Ilija attend these meetings? You said he was attending, if I understood correctly, all the time.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I probably wasn't there when this happened. What date was that meeting with Seselj exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is in April of 1991.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then I was there then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, you said he told you about it?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1991. I knew there was a meeting in Jagodnjak and Seselj was there. But I left in -- around about June the 19th, I got a flight. Actually I flew from Zagreb, I think, to go to my father' funeral and then I didn't come back until the October, so if there was meetings, I was aware then when the fighting started but I wasn't aware of how many meetings or what Ilija was doing during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So there is a meeting -- it's P70.50 that describes also a meeting in Beli Manastir around February 1991. Did you hear -- do you remember that one? You would have been there then.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, in 1991 we would have been in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You would have been in the --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- country.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: -- In Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we can take a look, I believe. If we could look at tab 3, Exhibit P70.50. And according to the records I have, this is an article from February 1991. Certainly in 1991. And I know that probably have trouble, and if we could go towards the middle. If you go to the very middle where it says: "One hour after the rally." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "So one hour after the rally" - and they're talking about a rally in another place - "protest was held in Beli Manastir also. One of the speakers said that Baranja has never been Croatian and that it won't be anymore and locals agreed with that."

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes, that was a general sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you aware that Goran Hadzic also made a distinction between Croats that he claimed were put in Baranja by Pavelic?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No. I was under the impression that or what Ilija told me was that Baranja was governed by -- Hungary during the Second World War and wasn't part of the Republic of Croatia and that's -- was his basis for saying that it's never been Croatian and very few Croats lived there according to the censuses. There were very few Croatians living in Baranja. There were mainly Serbs, Germans, Hungarians and Jewish people. So, no, I'm not aware of -- I didn't know Mr. Hadzic and I've never heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You didn't know Mr. Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you heard that he was a gentle soul. Where did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, that's what I heard from when people discussed. Other women, they discussed various people that were in charge or -- I never quite knew who was in charge anyway. They discussed people, and we gave our opinion about people, and -- and on one occasion Arkan came to visit, came there, into Baranja, after the war started and they said did I want to go and see him and I said -- I gave my opinion about him. But they had different opinions about him. They thought he was handsome, a bit like a pop star. I said I think he's a criminal. This is just what I said at the time. So we expressed opinions about people. Excuse me, the exception to that is Borivoje Zivanovic. I met him on several occasions, because he was at the slava we went to, so I've actually met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he worked sometimes, or actually a lot of time with Ilija Celar?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: He didn't work with him. Ilija was his interpreter and he called him on occasions when he needed an interpreter, in his words, that he could trust. That knew the language enough and not pretended to know the language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the war started, you say Arkan came to visit on one occasion. Do you recall when that was, was that in 1991 or in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It must have been while the fighting was still going on because I remember, that is, one of the wives was very upset, because she said Arkan had implemented a new law for the front line and that the men were there for ten days and got eight hours off to go home and get changed and do something, chop wood for their wives or whatever. And Arkan brought in a sort of law that for every minute that the man was late back to the front line he got a day in jail. And her husband had got 30 days in jail because he was 30 minutes late. So he was resented. That's all I know, apart from being asked if I wanted to go and look at him. That's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where was he going to be if he was going to be looked at?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: He was in the middle of Beli Manastir or somewhere. I don't know where because I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Turning now to Exhibit P144, which is tab 4. And if we could go to page 2 in the English, please, to the very top. And this is an interview with Goran Hadzic, and I wanted to focus on the section that starts: "The Croats." "The Croats, the native one, so-called Sokci, they are passive too, Croats, Herzegovina men, Dalmatians, even Zagorje men, all of them who settled after 1941, they are very dangerous, as they know that one of our goals when we gain control is to return all Pavelic volunteers." So were you familiar with the idea that those Croats who were considered Pavelic volunteers would be returned, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I wasn't aware there was any distinction, and both me and my husband were instrumental in ensuring that any Croats who wanted to stay could stay and if we could possibly help them, if they were being intimidated, we would try and get it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll get to that --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: It's not political about -- you know, I wasn't political. I have no idea what they were talking about, what they were saying. I didn't take any -- I didn't take notice of Milosevic either. I'm not a political person. I'm not interested in politics and I never have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document. I believe it is tab 66. It's P2955.2913. And I -- this is an article, and I believe the date that has been given to it is September of 1991. And I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I wasn't there then. I was in England.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. And I'd like to read this section: "People from Herzegovina, Imotska region and Zagorje, who were however colonised in our districts by Pavelic during the war will be given return tickets, said Hadzic. Further to the question, do you have problems with colonised Serbs who are extremists? Hadzic relied, no, we do not." You would agree with me that the return and return ticket concept here is the same as the one that I showed you right before this document?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't think that's an appropriate question for this witness. It involves a combination of speculation and conjecture and logical inference from the text in front of her, but not anything she knows or witnessed or learned about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that is exactly my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You were a bit of a media sensation when you came back and you were in Baranja because of the -- your testimony before parliament in 1991 and also you gave some interviews; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I was on Sky News, giving the situation as it was in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And locally I wanted to focus more on local journalists who were --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: In Baranja? Do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Or they could come from other places?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Journalists didn't come there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: There wasn't a local newspaper operating. I wasn't a sensation in Baranja. The only people that came to see me were a television crew brought by an English man from Belgrade to make a documentary programme about my living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. So I believe that will be tab 90. It's 65 ter 6568. And I wanted to go to 1 hour, 26 minutes, and 33 seconds, to 1 hour, 27 minutes, and 11 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Actually, for some context, let's begin at 1 hour, 24 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Although she has lived in Beli Manastir for quite a while, the English woman from our next report is more popular in the United Kingdom media than our own. Why is this, and what does she think about the Croatian army threatening to storm into Baranja? Vesna Ilic [phoen] has the report. We have come to Baranja to Beli Manastir to meet Amanda Brook who is more popular in Great Britain than she is here. Over there she delivers speeches in parliament and talks to television stations and newspapers in an effort to show the Serbian side of the current war. It was love that brought her to Osijek from Coventry, five years ago. She met Ilija Celar at a business meeting in Amsterdam and they have been together since. She happened to be in Beli Manastir's basement when the town was liberated. She was shocked with the fact ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Pause it right there she happened to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: First of all, is that the interview for the documentary that you had --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No, this is Serbian television. I -- I don't remember this at all. But the man I greeted at the gate was the English man, he is Serbian/English, he brought a film crew to make a film.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Michael Stojsalovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And there, the journalist says she happened to be in Beli Manastir's basement when the town was liberated?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: That's not true. I wasn't there. I was in England. She also says I appeared on numerous television programmes which is also untrue. They weren't interested in me in England. I mean, I was nobody really.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I was on Sky News because Bika Reid [phoen] arranged for me to be on Sky News. Other than that, I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where do you think they got the information that you happened to be in Beli Manastir's basement --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea, because it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The Serbian women were willing to commit group suicide rather than be captured by the Ustasha. Yes, I joined the Serbian lobby because I was ashamed and still am ashamed of the British media bias. I know I wouldn't be living with Serbs if they were capable of committing the atrocities they are being accused of. They publicised some of it on television and in newspapers but now when I wanted to speak about the Belgians, the foreign reporters are nowhere to be seen. I have spoken with the UNPROFOR commander, a Belgian man. He is openly anti-Serbian, as opposed to the Swedes, who are neutral. We come from old democracies, the Belgian man said. I told him that Belgium was 250 years old while the Serbian people had a tradition several centuries long. The latest attempts by Amanda Brook to inform the British people about the tragedy taking place in Croatia was the case of Franjo Sretkovic. Franjo is a Croat who was abducted in Zagreb only for being a Yugoslav, a Communist, and for being married to a Serb woman. They beat them in Osijek the same way they beat the Serbs. We, here, asked to exchange him. They let us have him for 6.000 German marks Franjo and I have written to the Times and Sky News. Franjo signed and was willing to testify. Nobody in Britain cared. I feared the arrival of the Croatian refugees because I believe Tudjman is capable of sacrificing his own refugees as an excuse to attack us. I know it is hard to leave your house but many of the local Croats were living in German-owned houses for being good Communists. Those houses are currently inhabited by Serbian refugees. If the army of the new democratic state of Croatia came, it would get rough. I would leave Baranja together with the Serbian women. Where would you live? In Serbia. In Belgrade? I don't like cities. I would definitely live in the countryside, in Serbia or in Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Celar, in this interview, you also reference local Croats being put in German owned houses for being good Communists?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why I said that. I was trying to make the point as I made in the British press, that opinion that when the British press was saying -- it was -- it's hard to judge that without seeing what I was responding to in the British press. I had written a lot of letters that weren't being published in the British press, and one of them was in answer to them saying that the Croatians had been forced out of Baranja and lost their homes and had lived there for centuries when in fact -- this is what I was responding to. At least I think it was that. That Baranja was a very special area that people had -- had been transient there. Most people hadn't been there for 50 years. They'd all been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the point of making that distinction? To drive home the fact that Croats didn't belong there any way?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I didn't say that that they didn't belong there. I meant if you took a Serbian perspective, that Croats had taken over other people's house and that somebody was now taking their house. That is what I was talking about. It was also a time of -- it tremendously stressful that time, very stressful that time. I can see how tired I was in that. That was done while the fighting was going on. This took place, didn't it, sometime after -- I don't know the date. But that is definitely at a time when -- before the mandate started. When the fighting was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: According to the information I have, this was around the time that there was talk about Croat refugees returning to the Baranja area. So this was in September, around September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, there was still shelling, I think, when that happened, when they did that. I don't -- it was a very emotive moment. Highly charged, emotional.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I -- I notice -- or heard that you were giving the interview in -- towards the end of 1992 in English.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you were speaking to a Serbo-Croatian speaker.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why didn't you -- you'd been there at that point, what, five -- five years. Why didn't you speak Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I didn't, because it's very different -- it's one thing to understand Serbian and speak Serbian but to give -- it's very hard to give specific opinions in Serbian. I've never had the language and still don't have that core language when you can adequately express emotion. It's still a basic -- well, I understand very well. Expressing myself is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the time that we have left, I'd like to take a step back and talk about the departure from Osijek in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- in April 1991 --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe leaving Osijek in paragraph 18, I believe, of your statement. Now from what I understand, it was Ilija Celar who told you that you and he had to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he was the one who told you that the police or the HOS had targeted him as a Serbian radical; right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he -- from your statement, it's not clear whether he believed he was targeted for arrest or killing, so it sounds very muddled. The information --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: If you were targeted in Croatia in those times, you didn't make the distinction about being arrested or being killed. To be targeted was frightening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who gave him this information?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, it was actually a Croatian policeman that worked in the police force in -- who we were friends with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what's the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: I never knew his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You never knew his name?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how do you know it was him?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, Ilija told me. But he didn't tell me his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So Ilija Celar said the Croatian policeman that I know told me that --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Rang me and told me this. And then my neighbour, when I subsequently rang Mitzi, who now lives in America. She's a Croatian. As I say, when I asked her to go and feed my cat the next day, she said she couldn't get near our house because it was surrounded by black-shirted men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in order to leave Osijek, you had time to organise a lorry?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What kind of lorry was it?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Just with a -- quite a big lorry with a flap at the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you were able to load your belongings onto this lorry?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And my question to you, Mrs. Celar, did you consider that you and Ilija Celar were voluntarily choosing to leave Osijek in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR
utterances.text: Well, I would say that we left because we were frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just given the line of questioning, I wonder if I could request that Your Honour give a particularly clear instruction to this witness regarding contacts with others. Just to make sure that there's no transgression of the requirements of the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Madam Celar, the Court, now adjourned for the day, we will continue your examination tomorrow at 9.00, and what I need to tell you, and what Mr. Gosnell asked me to underline, is that you continue to be a witness, even out of court, as long as you are on the stand, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anyone, and you can't have contact with either of the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that clear? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
